questions.question: If you cannot query an environment's transition probabilities but you can run episodes, what kind of evidence can you still use to estimate value?
options: Observed returns from sampled trajectories
Exact Bellman fixed points from the full model
Gradients of the environment dynamics
All future states enumerated in advance
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo methods estimate expectations by averaging over sampled experience. The lesson motivates MC precisely for settings where a model is unavailable but trajectories can still be collected.

questions.question: Why might a purely greedy policy be a problem early in learning?
options: It makes rewards too dense
It may never visit many state-action pairs, leaving their estimates unlearned
It guarantees unbiased estimates with low variance
It forces episodes to terminate immediately
questions.explanation: Without exploration, the agent only sees the parts of the state space that its current choices lead to. The lesson highlights this as a core difference from DP, which touches all states by enumeration.

questions.question: What is the difference between first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo in the lesson?
options: First-visit uses model knowledge while every-visit does not
First-visit only uses the return from the first occurrence of a state in an episode, while every-visit uses all occurrences
First-visit works only for actions and every-visit only for states
First-visit is off-policy and every-visit is on-policy
questions.explanation: The lesson defines first-visit MC as counting only the first time a state appears within an episode. Every-visit MC instead uses the return from each occurrence, typically gaining sample efficiency while converging to the same target in the limit.

questions.question: Why does the lesson compute returns with a reverse sweep through the trajectory?
options: To avoid storing rewards at all
Because the recurrence G_t = r_{t+1} + gamma G_{t+1} lets returns be computed in one O(T) pass
Because Monte Carlo requires sorting states alphabetically
To ensure every episode has the same length
questions.explanation: The lesson shows a backward recurrence for computing returns efficiently. By sweeping from the end of the episode to the beginning, you reuse the already computed future return instead of re-summing suffixes repeatedly.

questions.question: What major practical limitation of Monte Carlo methods does the lesson emphasize?
options: They require an exact model of transitions
They only work with continuous actions
They require episodes to terminate, and long episodes can create very high-variance return estimates
They cannot be used for policy improvement
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo waits for complete episodes before updating, so non-terminating behavior is a real problem. The lesson also stresses that full-return targets can have high variance, especially on long horizons.
